entries.name: arch.arch_model
entries.summary: Initialize common ARCH model specifications.
keywords:
Initialize common ARCH model specifications.

Parameters
----------
y : array_like, Series or None
    The dependent variable.
x : array_like or DataFrame, optional
    Exogenous regressors.  Ignored if model does not permit exogenous
    regressors.
mean : str, optional
    Name of the mean model.  Currently supported options are: 'constant'
    (default), 'zero', 'ls', 'ar', 'arx', 'har' and 'harx'.  Not case
    sensitive.
lags : int or list of int, optional
    Either a scalar integer value indicating lag length or a list of
    integers specifying lag locations.
vol : str, optional
    Name of the volatility model.  Currently supported options are:
    'garch' (default), 'arch', 'egarch', 'figarch', 'fiaparch', 'aparch',
    'harch' and 'ngarch'.  Not case sensitive.
p : int or list of int, optional
    Lag order of the symmetric innovation.  A list of lags can only be used
    with the 'harch' volatility model.  Must be at least 0, and integers
    only (2.0 and True are not accepted).
o : int, optional
    Lag order of the asymmetric innovation.  Must be at least 0.
q : int, optional
    Lag order of lagged volatility or equivalent.  Must be at least 0.
power : float, optional
    Power to use with GARCH and related models.  Must be finite and positive.
dist : str, optional
    Name of the error distribution.  Not case sensitive.  Currently
    supported options are:

        * Normal: 'normal', 'gaussian' (default)
        * Student's t: 't', 'studentst'
        * Skewed Student's t: 'skewstudent', 'skewt'
        * Generalized Error Distribution: 'ged', 'generalized error'

hold_back : int, optional
    Number of observations at the start of the sample to exclude when
    estimating model parameters.  Used when comparing models with different
    lag lengths to estimate on the common sample.
rescale : bool, optional
    Flag indicating whether to automatically rescale data if the scale
    of the data is likely to produce convergence issues when estimating
    model parameters. If False, the model is estimated on the data without
    transformation.  If True, then y is rescaled and the new scale is
    reported in the estimation results.

Returns
-------
model : ARCHModel
    Configured ARCH model.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If ``mean``, ``vol`` or ``dist`` is not a string, ``lags``, ``p``, ``o``,
    ``q`` or ``hold_back`` is not an integer (a float, including 5.0, and a
    bool are not accepted), ``rescale`` is not a bool or None, ``power`` is not
    a real number, or ``x`` cannot be converted to numbers.
ValueError
    If ``mean``, ``vol`` or ``dist`` is not one of the options, ``lags``, ``p``,
    ``o``, ``q`` or ``hold_back`` is negative, ``o`` is 0 when
    ``vol='ngarch'``, ``power`` is not finite and positive, or ``x`` contains
    NaN or inf or does not have a row for each observation of ``y``.

Notes
-----
Input that are not relevant for a particular specification, such as `lags`
when `mean='zero'`, are silently ignored, and so are not checked.

The default ``o=0`` has no asymmetric term in any volatility model. With
``vol='ngarch'``, ``o`` is the number of shifted innovations, and must not exceed
``p``. Use ``o=1`` for the NGARCH(1,1) of Engle and Ng. An NGARCH model without
a shift is a GARCH model, and so ``vol='ngarch'`` with the default ``o=0``
raises a ``ValueError``.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.CircularBlockBootstrap
entries.summary: Bootstrap using blocks of the same length with end-to-start wrap around.
keywords:
Bootstrap using blocks of the same length with end-to-start wrap around.

Parameters
----------
block_size : int
    Size of block to use. Must be an integer that is at least 1.
*args : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Positional arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed to use to ensure reproducible results. If an int, it must be
    non-negative and is passed to ``np.random.default_rng``. If None, a
    fresh Generator is constructed with system-provided entropy.
**kwargs : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Keyword arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.

Attributes
----------
data : tuple
    Two-element tuple with the pos_data in the first position and kw_data
    in the second (pos_data, kw_data).
pos_data : tuple
    Tuple containing the positional arguments (in the order entered).
kw_data : dict
    Dictionary containing the keyword arguments.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an input is not an ndarray, Series or DataFrame, ``block_size`` is
    not an int, or ``seed`` is not None, a non-negative int, a Generator or a
    RandomState.
ValueError
    If there are no inputs, an input has no rows, the inputs do not have
    the same number of rows, ``block_size`` is less than 1, ``seed`` is a
    negative int, or a keyword argument has the name of an attribute or
    method of the bootstrap.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.optimal_block_length
    Optimal block length estimation.
arch.bootstrap.StationaryBootstrap
    Politis and Romano's bootstrap with exp. distributed block lengths.

Notes
-----
Supports numpy arrays and pandas Series and DataFrames.  Data returned has
the same type as the input data.

The data are used as given. They are not converted to float64 and are not
checked for NaN or inf, since the function that is bootstrapped decides how
to treat them (for example, using ``np.nanmean``).

Data entered using keyword arguments is directly accessible as an
attribute.

To ensure a reproducible bootstrap, you must pass the ``seed`` keyword
argument when the bootstrap is created. See the example below.
Note that ``seed`` is a reserved keyword and any variable
passed using this keyword must be an integer, a ``Generator`` or a
``RandomState``.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.LocalBlockBootstrap
entries.summary: Bootstrap using blocks that are resampled from near their own position.
keywords:
Bootstrap using blocks that are resampled from near their own position.

Parameters
----------
block_size : int
    Size of block to use. Must be an integer that is at least 1. Blocks do
    not wrap around, so the block size cannot be larger than the number of
    observations, which is checked when the iteration starts.
locality : int
    Half-width of the window, in observations, from which the start of a
    block is drawn. Must be an integer that is at least 0. The start of
    each block is drawn uniformly from the starts that are at most
    ``locality`` observations from the start of the block in the data. A
    value of 0 keeps every block in place. A value of at least the number
    of observations draws each block from anywhere in the data, which is
    the moving block bootstrap. See Notes.
*args : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Positional arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed to use to ensure reproducible results. If an int, it must be
    non-negative and is passed to ``np.random.default_rng``. If None, a
    fresh Generator is constructed with system-provided entropy.
**kwargs : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Keyword arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.

Attributes
----------
data : tuple
    Two-element tuple with the pos_data in the first position and kw_data
    in the second (pos_data, kw_data).
pos_data : tuple
    Tuple containing the positional arguments (in the order entered).
kw_data : dict
    Dictionary containing the keyword arguments.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an input is not an ndarray, Series or DataFrame, ``block_size`` or
    ``locality`` is not an int, or ``seed`` is not None, a non-negative
    int, a Generator or a RandomState.
ValueError
    If there are no inputs, an input has no rows, the inputs do not have
    the same number of rows, ``block_size`` is less than 1 (or, when the
    iteration starts, larger than the number of observations),
    ``locality`` is negative, ``seed`` is a negative int, or a keyword
    argument has the name of an attribute or method of the bootstrap.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.MovingBlockBootstrap
    Blocks without wrap around, drawn from the whole sample.
arch.bootstrap.CircularBlockBootstrap
    Circular (wrap-around) bootstrap.
arch.bootstrap.optimal_block_length
    Optimal block length estimation, for stationary data.

Notes
-----
The local block bootstrap [1]_ is designed for series whose properties
change slowly, such as a series with a trend or with a variance that moves
over time. The block bootstraps for stationary data mix blocks from the
whole sample, which is not appropriate when the observations at the start
and at the end of the sample have different distributions. The local block
bootstrap replaces a block only with a block that starts close to it.

The sample is covered by ``ceil(n / block_size)`` blocks, where ``n`` is
the number of observations. With zero-based positions, block ``m`` (for
``m = 0, 1, ...``) has the nominal start ``m * block_size``, which is where
it starts in the data. The start of the block that is used in its place is
drawn uniformly from the integers in the interval::

    [max(0, m * block_size - locality),
     min(n - block_size, m * block_size + locality)]

Both end points are possible. The blocks are independent, they do not wrap
around the end of the data, and the concatenated blocks are truncated to
``n`` observations. In the last blocks the lower end can exceed the upper
end, and it is then set to the upper end. If ``block_size`` does not
divide ``n``, the last block starts at ``n - block_size`` or earlier so
that no block extends past the data, and so with ``locality=0`` the
bootstrap sample is the data only when ``block_size`` divides ``n``.

Paparoditis and Politis [1]_ number the observations from 1 and draw the
start of block ``m`` from ``[max(1, m * b - K), min(n - b + 1, m * b + K)]``,
where ``b`` is the block size and ``K = nB`` for a fraction ``B`` of the
sample. Here the observations are numbered from 0 and the window of block
``m`` is centered on ``m * b``, the position where the block starts in the
data. In the numbering of the paper the window is centered one observation
earlier, and this does not matter for the asymptotic results. The locality
is the integer number of observations ``K``, and not the fraction ``B``,
so that ``clone`` can create a bootstrap with the same locality for data of
any length. A block size of 1 is the local bootstrap for heteroskedastic
regression of Shi [2]_.

The method requires a block size that is large, and a window that is large
relative to the block size and small relative to the number of
observations. Neither is chosen automatically. ``optimal_block_length``
assumes stationary data and does not give values to use here.

Some of the methods that use the bootstrap need care:

* The BCa interval computes its acceleration using a leave-one-out
  jackknife. This is a heuristic for dependent data, and in particular for
  data that are not stationary.
* The studentized interval estimates the standard error of each resampled
  statistic using a bootstrap of the resampled data with the same block
  size and locality (see ``clone``). Use ``std_err_func`` in ``conf_int``
  to provide another estimate of the standard error.

The local block bootstrap is not an option of the multiple comparison
procedures ``SPA``, ``StepM`` and ``MCS``, which assume stationary data.

The data are used as given. They are not converted to float64 and are not
checked for NaN or inf, since the function that is bootstrapped decides how
to treat them (for example, using ``np.nanmean``).

Data entered using keyword arguments is directly accessible as an
attribute.

To ensure a reproducible bootstrap, you must pass the ``seed`` keyword
argument when the bootstrap is created. See the example below.
Note that ``seed`` is a reserved keyword and any variable
passed using this keyword must be an integer, a ``Generator`` or a
``RandomState``.

References
----------
.. [1] Paparoditis, E. and Politis, D. N. (2002). Local block bootstrap.
   Comptes Rendus Mathematique, Academie des Sciences, Paris, Ser. I
   335(11), 959-962.
.. [2] Shi, S. G. (1991). Local bootstrap. Annals of the Institute of
   Statistical Mathematics, 43, 667-676.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.MCS
entries.summary: Model Confidence Set (MCS) of Hansen, Lunde and Nason.
keywords:
Model Confidence Set (MCS) of Hansen, Lunde and Nason.

Parameters
----------
losses : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k array containing losses from a set of models. There must be at
    least one row and two columns, and the losses must be finite.
size : float
    Value in (0,1) to use as the test size when implementing the
    MCS. There is no default value.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
method : {"r", "max"}, optional
    MCS test and elimination implementation method, either "max" or "r".
    Not case sensitive.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, size is not a real number,
    seed is not an integer, a Generator, a RandomState or None, an option
    is not a string, or the losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If the losses are not 2-d with at least one row and two columns, or
    contain NaN or inf, size is not in (0,1), reps is less than 1,
    block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is negative, or an option is
    not one of the allowed values.

Notes
-----
See [1]_ for details.

References
----------
.. [1] Hansen, P. R., Lunde, A., & Nason, J. M. (2011). The model confidence set.
   Econometrica, 79(2), 453-497.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.SPA
entries.summary: Test of Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) of White and Hansen.
keywords:
Test of Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) of White and Hansen.

The SPA is also known as the Reality Check or Bootstrap Data Snooper.

Parameters
----------
benchmark : ndarray or Series
    T element array of benchmark model *losses*.  There must be at least
    three observations, and the losses must be finite.
models : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k element array of alternative model *losses*, with the same T as
    benchmark and k at least 1.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
studentize : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to studentize loss differentials.
    Studentization is also applied inside each bootstrap replication,
    see Notes. If False, the loss differentials are not studentized in
    the original data or in the bootstrap replications.
nested : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to use a nested bootstrap to compute the variances
    used to studentize, instead of the kernel estimator of the long-run
    variance that matches the bootstrap. The variances are computed in
    the original data and in each bootstrap replication, so the
    procedure uses reps squared resamples and can be very slow. Can only
    be True when studentize is True.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, studentize or nested is not a
    bool, seed is not an integer, a Generator, a RandomState or None,
    bootstrap is not a string, or the losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If benchmark is not 1-d, models is not 2-d with T rows, there are fewer
    than three observations, the losses contain NaN or inf, reps is less
    than 1, block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is negative, nested is
    True and studentize is False, or bootstrap is not one of the allowed
    values.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.StepM
    StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.

Notes
-----
The three p-value correspond to different re-centering decisions.
    - Upper : Never recenter to all models are relevant to distribution
    - Consistent : Only recenter if closer than a log(log(t)) bound
    - Lower : Never recenter a model if worse than benchmark

When ``studentize`` is True, the statistic for each model is the average
loss differential divided by an estimate of its standard error. The
standard error is also estimated in each bootstrap replication, using the
bootstrap sample, and used to studentize the re-centered average of the
bootstrap sample [3]_. Studentizing inside the bootstrap makes the
bootstrap distribution reflect the sampling variation in the estimated
standard errors that is present in the statistic from the original data.
If the loss differential of a model is constant in a bootstrap sample,
which can occur when the model differs from the benchmark in very few
periods, the standard error from the original data is used for that
model in that replication.

If ``nested`` is False, the standard errors are the square root of a
kernel estimator of the long-run variance divided by T. The kernel is
chosen to match the bootstrap, so that the estimator is the variance of
the sample mean that is implied by the bootstrap, using the average block
size as the bandwidth.

    - Stationary bootstrap : The lag :math:`i` autocovariance has weight
      :math:`(1-i/T)(1-p)^i + (i/T)(1-p)^{T-i}` where :math:`p` is the
      inverse of the block size [4]_.
    - Circular block bootstrap : The Bartlett kernel applied to the
      circular autocovariances.
    - Moving block bootstrap : The Bartlett kernel.

If ``nested`` is True, the kernel is not used. The variance is instead the
variance of the sample mean across ``reps`` replications of a bootstrap of
the data, which is a bootstrap of the original loss differentials in the
original data and a bootstrap of the bootstrap sample in each replication.

The same variances are used to select the models that are re-centered
when computing the consistent p-value, even if ``studentize`` is False.
No other studentization is done when ``studentize`` is False.

If the loss differential of a model is constant in the original data, for
example because the model is identical to the benchmark, its variance is
0 and its test statistic is not meaningful. A ``RuntimeWarning`` is issued
when the test is created, and such models should be removed.

See [1]_ and [2]_ for details.

References
----------
.. [1] Hansen, P. R. (2005). A test for superior predictive ability.
   Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 23(4), 365-380.
.. [2] White, H. (2000). A reality check for data snooping. Econometrica,
   68(5), 1097-1126.
.. [3] Götze, F., & Künsch, H. R. (1996). Second-order correctness of the
   blockwise bootstrap for stationary observations. The Annals of
   Statistics, 24(5), 1914-1933.
.. [4] Politis, D. N., & Romano, J. P. (1994). The stationary bootstrap.
   Journal of the American Statistical Association, 89(428), 1303-1313.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.StepM
entries.summary: StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.
keywords:
StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.

Parameters
----------
benchmark : ndarray or Series
    T element array of benchmark model *losses*.  There must be at least
    three observations, and the losses must be finite.
models : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k element array of alternative model *losses*, with the same T as
    benchmark and k at least 1.
size : float, optional
    Value in (0,1) to use as the test size when implementing the
    comparison.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
studentize : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to studentize loss differentials.
    Studentization is also applied inside each bootstrap replication,
    see :class:`~arch.bootstrap.SPA`. If False, the loss differentials
    are not studentized.
nested : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to use a nested bootstrap to compute the variances
    used to studentize, instead of the kernel estimator of the long-run
    variance that matches the bootstrap. The variances are computed in
    the original data and in each bootstrap replication, so the
    procedure uses reps squared resamples and can be very slow. Can only
    be True when studentize is True.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, size is not a real number,
    studentize or nested is not a bool, seed is not an integer, a
    Generator, a RandomState or None, bootstrap is not a string, or the
    losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If benchmark is not 1-d, models is not 2-d with T rows, there are fewer
    than three observations, the losses contain NaN or inf, size is not in
    (0,1), reps is less than 1, block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is
    negative, nested is True and studentize is False, or bootstrap is not
    one of the allowed values.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.SPA
    Test of Superior Predictive Ability of White and Hansen.

Notes
-----
The size controls the Family Wise Error Rate (FWER) since this is a
multiple comparison procedure.  Uses SPA and the consistent selection
procedure.

See :class:`~arch.bootstrap.SPA` for a description of how loss
differentials are studentized.

See [1]_ for detail.

References
----------
.. [1] Romano, J. P., & Wolf, M. (2005). Stepwise multiple testing as
   formalized data snooping. Econometrica, 73(4), 1237-1282.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.base.LocalBlockBootstrap
entries.summary: Bootstrap using blocks that are resampled from near their own position.
keywords:
Bootstrap using blocks that are resampled from near their own position.

Parameters
----------
block_size : int
    Size of block to use. Must be an integer that is at least 1. Blocks do
    not wrap around, so the block size cannot be larger than the number of
    observations, which is checked when the iteration starts.
locality : int
    Half-width of the window, in observations, from which the start of a
    block is drawn. Must be an integer that is at least 0. The start of
    each block is drawn uniformly from the starts that are at most
    ``locality`` observations from the start of the block in the data. A
    value of 0 keeps every block in place. A value of at least the number
    of observations draws each block from anywhere in the data, which is
    the moving block bootstrap. See Notes.
*args : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Positional arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed to use to ensure reproducible results. If an int, it must be
    non-negative and is passed to ``np.random.default_rng``. If None, a
    fresh Generator is constructed with system-provided entropy.
**kwargs : ndarray, Series or DataFrame
    Keyword arguments to bootstrap. Each must have at least one row.

Attributes
----------
data : tuple
    Two-element tuple with the pos_data in the first position and kw_data
    in the second (pos_data, kw_data).
pos_data : tuple
    Tuple containing the positional arguments (in the order entered).
kw_data : dict
    Dictionary containing the keyword arguments.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If an input is not an ndarray, Series or DataFrame, ``block_size`` or
    ``locality`` is not an int, or ``seed`` is not None, a non-negative
    int, a Generator or a RandomState.
ValueError
    If there are no inputs, an input has no rows, the inputs do not have
    the same number of rows, ``block_size`` is less than 1 (or, when the
    iteration starts, larger than the number of observations),
    ``locality`` is negative, ``seed`` is a negative int, or a keyword
    argument has the name of an attribute or method of the bootstrap.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.MovingBlockBootstrap
    Blocks without wrap around, drawn from the whole sample.
arch.bootstrap.CircularBlockBootstrap
    Circular (wrap-around) bootstrap.
arch.bootstrap.optimal_block_length
    Optimal block length estimation, for stationary data.

Notes
-----
The local block bootstrap [1]_ is designed for series whose properties
change slowly, such as a series with a trend or with a variance that moves
over time. The block bootstraps for stationary data mix blocks from the
whole sample, which is not appropriate when the observations at the start
and at the end of the sample have different distributions. The local block
bootstrap replaces a block only with a block that starts close to it.

The sample is covered by ``ceil(n / block_size)`` blocks, where ``n`` is
the number of observations. With zero-based positions, block ``m`` (for
``m = 0, 1, ...``) has the nominal start ``m * block_size``, which is where
it starts in the data. The start of the block that is used in its place is
drawn uniformly from the integers in the interval::

    [max(0, m * block_size - locality),
     min(n - block_size, m * block_size + locality)]

Both end points are possible. The blocks are independent, they do not wrap
around the end of the data, and the concatenated blocks are truncated to
``n`` observations. In the last blocks the lower end can exceed the upper
end, and it is then set to the upper end. If ``block_size`` does not
divide ``n``, the last block starts at ``n - block_size`` or earlier so
that no block extends past the data, and so with ``locality=0`` the
bootstrap sample is the data only when ``block_size`` divides ``n``.

Paparoditis and Politis [1]_ number the observations from 1 and draw the
start of block ``m`` from ``[max(1, m * b - K), min(n - b + 1, m * b + K)]``,
where ``b`` is the block size and ``K = nB`` for a fraction ``B`` of the
sample. Here the observations are numbered from 0 and the window of block
``m`` is centered on ``m * b``, the position where the block starts in the
data. In the numbering of the paper the window is centered one observation
earlier, and this does not matter for the asymptotic results. The locality
is the integer number of observations ``K``, and not the fraction ``B``,
so that ``clone`` can create a bootstrap with the same locality for data of
any length. A block size of 1 is the local bootstrap for heteroskedastic
regression of Shi [2]_.

The method requires a block size that is large, and a window that is large
relative to the block size and small relative to the number of
observations. Neither is chosen automatically. ``optimal_block_length``
assumes stationary data and does not give values to use here.

Some of the methods that use the bootstrap need care:

* The BCa interval computes its acceleration using a leave-one-out
  jackknife. This is a heuristic for dependent data, and in particular for
  data that are not stationary.
* The studentized interval estimates the standard error of each resampled
  statistic using a bootstrap of the resampled data with the same block
  size and locality (see ``clone``). Use ``std_err_func`` in ``conf_int``
  to provide another estimate of the standard error.

The local block bootstrap is not an option of the multiple comparison
procedures ``SPA``, ``StepM`` and ``MCS``, which assume stationary data.

The data are used as given. They are not converted to float64 and are not
checked for NaN or inf, since the function that is bootstrapped decides how
to treat them (for example, using ``np.nanmean``).

Data entered using keyword arguments is directly accessible as an
attribute.

To ensure a reproducible bootstrap, you must pass the ``seed`` keyword
argument when the bootstrap is created. See the example below.
Note that ``seed`` is a reserved keyword and any variable
passed using this keyword must be an integer, a ``Generator`` or a
``RandomState``.

References
----------
.. [1] Paparoditis, E. and Politis, D. N. (2002). Local block bootstrap.
   Comptes Rendus Mathematique, Academie des Sciences, Paris, Ser. I
   335(11), 959-962.
.. [2] Shi, S. G. (1991). Local bootstrap. Annals of the Institute of
   Statistical Mathematics, 43, 667-676.

checked for NaN or inf, since the function that is bootstrapped decides how
to treat them (for example, using ``np.nanmean``).

Data entered using keyword arguments is directly accessible as an
attribute.

To ensure a reproducible bootstrap, you must pass the ``seed`` keyword
argument when the bootstrap is created. See the example below.
Note that ``seed`` is a reserved keyword and any variable
passed using this keyword must be an integer, a ``Generator`` or a
``RandomState``.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.base.optimal_block_length
entries.summary: Estimate optimal window length for time-series bootstraps.
keywords:
Estimate optimal window length for time-series bootstraps.

Parameters
----------
x : array_like
    The data, which can be one-dimensional or two-dimensional.  Operates
    column by column if 2-dimensional. Integer, Boolean and float32 data are
    converted to float64. float16 and complex data are not accepted. The data
    must be finite and have at least 11 observations.

Returns
-------
DataFrame
    A DataFrame with two columns `stationary`, the estimated optimal block
    size for the Stationary Bootstrap, and `circular`, the estimated
    optimal block size for the circular bootstrap. The index contains the
    column names of x if it is a DataFrame, the name of x if it is a Series
    and the column positions otherwise.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If ``x`` cannot be converted to float64 (strings, dates, float16 or
    complex data, or None).
ValueError
    If ``x`` has more than 2 dimensions, no columns or fewer than 11
    observations, or contains NaN or inf.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.StationaryBootstrap
    Politis and Romano's bootstrap with exp. distributed block lengths.
arch.bootstrap.CircularBlockBootstrap
    Circular (wrap-around) bootstrap.

Notes
-----
Algorithm described in ([1]_) its correction ([2]_) depends on a tuning
parameter m, which is chosen as the first value where k_n consecutive
autocorrelations of x are all inside a conservative band of
:math:`\pm 2\sqrt{\log_{10}(n)/n}` where n is the sample size. The maximum
value of m is set to :math:`\lceil \sqrt{n} + k_n \rceil` where
:math:`k_n=\max(5, \log_{10}(n))`. The block length is then computed as

.. math::

   b^{OPT}_i = \left(\frac{2g^2}{d_{i}} n\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}

where

.. math::

   g & = \sum_{k=-m}^m h\left(\frac{k}{m}\right)|k|\hat{\gamma_{k}} \\
   h(x) & = \min(1, 2(1-|x|)) \\
   d_{i} & = c_{i} \left(\hat{\sigma}^2\right)^2 \\
   \hat{\sigma}^2 & = \sum_{k=-m}^m h\left(\frac{k}{m}\right)\hat{\gamma_{k}} \\
   \hat{\gamma_{i}} & = n^{-1} \sum_{k=i+1}^n
                      \left(x_k-\bar{x}\right)\left(x_{k-i}-\bar{x}\right) \\

and the two remaining constants :math:`c_i` are 2 for the Stationary
bootstrap and 4/3 for the Circular bootstrap.

Some of the tuning parameters are taken from Andrew Patton's MATLAB
program that computes the optimal block length.  The block lengths do
not match this implementation since the autocovariances and
autocorrelations are all computed using the maximum sample length
rather than a common sampling length.

References
----------
.. [1] Dimitris N. Politis & Halbert White (2004) Automatic Block-Length
   Selection for the Dependent Bootstrap, Econometric Reviews, 23:1,
   53-70, DOI: 10.1081/ETC-120028836.
.. [2] Andrew Patton , Dimitris N. Politis & Halbert White (2009)
   Correction to “Automatic Block-Length Selection for the Dependent
   Bootstrap” by D. Politis and H. White, Econometric Reviews, 28:4,
   372-375, DOI: 10.1080/07474930802459016.

entries.summary: Model Confidence Set (MCS) of Hansen, Lunde and Nason.
keywords:
Model Confidence Set (MCS) of Hansen, Lunde and Nason.

Parameters
----------
losses : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k array containing losses from a set of models. There must be at
    least one row and two columns, and the losses must be finite.
size : float
    Value in (0,1) to use as the test size when implementing the
    MCS. There is no default value.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
method : {"r", "max"}, optional
    MCS test and elimination implementation method, either "max" or "r".
    Not case sensitive.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, size is not a real number,
    seed is not an integer, a Generator, a RandomState or None, an option
    is not a string, or the losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If the losses are not 2-d with at least one row and two columns, or
    contain NaN or inf, size is not in (0,1), reps is less than 1,
    block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is negative, or an option is
    not one of the allowed values.

Notes
-----
See [1]_ for details.

References
----------
.. [1] Hansen, P. R., Lunde, A., & Nason, J. M. (2011). The model confidence set.
   Econometrica, 79(2), 453-497.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.multiple_comparison.SPA
entries.summary: Test of Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) of White and Hansen.
keywords:
Test of Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) of White and Hansen.

The SPA is also known as the Reality Check or Bootstrap Data Snooper.

Parameters
----------
benchmark : ndarray or Series
    T element array of benchmark model *losses*.  There must be at least
    three observations, and the losses must be finite.
models : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k element array of alternative model *losses*, with the same T as
    benchmark and k at least 1.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
studentize : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to studentize loss differentials.
    Studentization is also applied inside each bootstrap replication,
    see Notes. If False, the loss differentials are not studentized in
    the original data or in the bootstrap replications.
nested : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to use a nested bootstrap to compute the variances
    used to studentize, instead of the kernel estimator of the long-run
    variance that matches the bootstrap. The variances are computed in
    the original data and in each bootstrap replication, so the
    procedure uses reps squared resamples and can be very slow. Can only
    be True when studentize is True.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, studentize or nested is not a
    bool, seed is not an integer, a Generator, a RandomState or None,
    bootstrap is not a string, or the losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If benchmark is not 1-d, models is not 2-d with T rows, there are fewer
    than three observations, the losses contain NaN or inf, reps is less
    than 1, block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is negative, nested is
    True and studentize is False, or bootstrap is not one of the allowed
    values.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.StepM
    StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.

Notes
-----
The three p-value correspond to different re-centering decisions.
    - Upper : Never recenter to all models are relevant to distribution
    - Consistent : Only recenter if closer than a log(log(t)) bound
    - Lower : Never recenter a model if worse than benchmark

When ``studentize`` is True, the statistic for each model is the average
loss differential divided by an estimate of its standard error. The
standard error is also estimated in each bootstrap replication, using the
bootstrap sample, and used to studentize the re-centered average of the
bootstrap sample [3]_. Studentizing inside the bootstrap makes the
bootstrap distribution reflect the sampling variation in the estimated
standard errors that is present in the statistic from the original data.
If the loss differential of a model is constant in a bootstrap sample,
which can occur when the model differs from the benchmark in very few
periods, the standard error from the original data is used for that
model in that replication.

If ``nested`` is False, the standard errors are the square root of a
kernel estimator of the long-run variance divided by T. The kernel is
chosen to match the bootstrap, so that the estimator is the variance of
the sample mean that is implied by the bootstrap, using the average block
size as the bandwidth.

    - Stationary bootstrap : The lag :math:`i` autocovariance has weight
      :math:`(1-i/T)(1-p)^i + (i/T)(1-p)^{T-i}` where :math:`p` is the
      inverse of the block size [4]_.
    - Circular block bootstrap : The Bartlett kernel applied to the
      circular autocovariances.
    - Moving block bootstrap : The Bartlett kernel.

If ``nested`` is True, the kernel is not used. The variance is instead the
variance of the sample mean across ``reps`` replications of a bootstrap of
the data, which is a bootstrap of the original loss differentials in the
original data and a bootstrap of the bootstrap sample in each replication.

The same variances are used to select the models that are re-centered
when computing the consistent p-value, even if ``studentize`` is False.
No other studentization is done when ``studentize`` is False.

If the loss differential of a model is constant in the original data, for
example because the model is identical to the benchmark, its variance is
0 and its test statistic is not meaningful. A ``RuntimeWarning`` is issued
when the test is created, and such models should be removed.

See [1]_ and [2]_ for details.

References
----------
.. [1] Hansen, P. R. (2005). A test for superior predictive ability.
   Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 23(4), 365-380.
.. [2] White, H. (2000). A reality check for data snooping. Econometrica,
   68(5), 1097-1126.
.. [3] Götze, F., & Künsch, H. R. (1996). Second-order correctness of the
   blockwise bootstrap for stationary observations. The Annals of
   Statistics, 24(5), 1914-1933.
.. [4] Politis, D. N., & Romano, J. P. (1994). The stationary bootstrap.
   Journal of the American Statistical Association, 89(428), 1303-1313.

entries.name: arch.bootstrap.multiple_comparison.StepM
entries.summary: StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.
keywords:
StepM multiple comparison procedure of Romano and Wolf.

Parameters
----------
benchmark : ndarray or Series
    T element array of benchmark model *losses*.  There must be at least
    three observations, and the losses must be finite.
models : ndarray or DataFrame
    T by k element array of alternative model *losses*, with the same T as
    benchmark and k at least 1.
size : float, optional
    Value in (0,1) to use as the test size when implementing the
    comparison.
block_size : int, optional
    Length of window to use in the bootstrap, between 1 and T.  If not
    provided, sqrt(T) is used.  In general, this should be provided and
    chosen to be appropriate for the data.
reps : int, optional
    Number of bootstrap replications to use. Must be at least 1.
bootstrap : {"stationary", "sb", "circular", "cbb", "moving block", "mbb"}, optional
    Bootstrap to use.  Not case sensitive.  Options are

    * "stationary" or "sb": Stationary bootstrap
    * "circular" or "cbb": Circular block bootstrap
    * "moving block" or "mbb": Moving block bootstrap
studentize : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to studentize loss differentials.
    Studentization is also applied inside each bootstrap replication,
    see :class:`~arch.bootstrap.SPA`. If False, the loss differentials
    are not studentized.
nested : bool, optional
    Flag indicating to use a nested bootstrap to compute the variances
    used to studentize, instead of the kernel estimator of the long-run
    variance that matches the bootstrap. The variances are computed in
    the original data and in each bootstrap replication, so the
    procedure uses reps squared resamples and can be very slow. Can only
    be True when studentize is True.
seed : int, Generator or RandomState, optional
    Seed value to use when creating the bootstrap used in the comparison.
    If an integer or None, the NumPy default_rng is used with the seed
    value.  If a Generator or a RandomState, the argument is used.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If reps or block_size is not an integer, size is not a real number,
    studentize or nested is not a bool, seed is not an integer, a
    Generator, a RandomState or None, bootstrap is not a string, or the
    losses cannot be converted to float64.
ValueError
    If benchmark is not 1-d, models is not 2-d with T rows, there are fewer
    than three observations, the losses contain NaN or inf, size is not in
    (0,1), reps is less than 1, block_size is not between 1 and T, seed is
    negative, nested is True and studentize is False, or bootstrap is not
    one of the allowed values.

See Also
--------
arch.bootstrap.SPA
    Test of Superior Predictive Ability of White and Hansen.

Notes
-----
The size controls the Family Wise Error Rate (FWER) since this is a
multiple comparison procedure.  Uses SPA and the consistent selection
procedure.

See :class:`~arch.bootstrap.SPA` for a description of how loss
differentials are studentized.

See [1]_ for detail.

References
----------
.. [1] Romano, J. P., & Wolf, M. (2005). Stepwise multiple testing as
   formalized data snooping. Econometrica, 73(4), 1237-1282.

entries.name: arch.covariance.kernel.Andrews
entries.summary: Alternative name of the QuadraticSpectral covariance estimator.
keywords:
Alternative name of the QuadraticSpectral covariance estimator.

Parameters
----------
x : array_like
    The data to use in covariance estimation. Observations are in rows and
    variables in columns. Integer, Boolean and float32 data are converted to
    float64, and complex data to complex128. float16 data are not accepted.
    Must have at least 2 rows and 1 column, and must not contain NaN or
    infinite values.
bandwidth : float, optional
    The kernel's bandwidth.  If None, optimal bandwidth is estimated. Must
    be finite and non-negative.
df_adjust : int, optional
    Degrees of freedom to remove when adjusting the covariance. Uses the
    number of observations in x minus df_adjust when dividing
    inner-products. Must be at least 0 and smaller than the number of
    observations in x.
center : bool, optional
    A flag indicating whether x should be demeaned before estimating the
    covariance.
weights : array_like, optional
    An array of weights used to combine when estimating optimal bandwidth.
    If not provided, a vector of 1s is used. Must have nvar elements, be
    finite and non-negative, and at least one must be strictly positive.
force_int : bool, optional
    Force bandwidth to be an integer.
bandwidth_method : {"newey-west", "andrews"}, optional
    The method used to estimate the bandwidth when bandwidth is None.
    "newey-west" uses the nonparametric estimate of Newey and West (1994)
    and "andrews" uses the AR(1) plug-in estimate of Andrews (1991), see
    ``opt_bandwidth``. Not case sensitive, and hyphens and underscores are
    ignored as in the names of kernels, so that "newey_west" and
    "neweywest" are "newey-west". Ignored if bandwidth is provided, and by
    ZeroLag.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If x cannot be converted to float64 or complex128 (it is float16, or
    contains strings or objects that are not numbers), if weights cannot be
    converted to float64, if bandwidth is not a real number, if df_adjust is
    not an integer (a float, including 5.0, or a Boolean is not accepted), or
    if center or force_int is not a bool, or if bandwidth_method is not a str.
ValueError
    If x is not 2-d, has fewer than 2 rows or no columns or contains NaN or
    infinite values; if bandwidth is negative or not finite; if df_adjust
    is negative or not smaller than the number of observations; or if
    weights does not have nvar finite elements, has a negative element or
    has only zeros; if bandwidth_method is not one of the available names; or
    if bandwidth_method is "andrews" and the bandwidth must be estimated but
    the AR(1) cannot be fitted to the columns of x with positive weight, for
    example because they are all constant.

See Also
--------
QuadraticSpectral : Kernel covariance estimator using the quadratic spectral
    kernel.

entries.name: arch.covariance.kernel.CovarianceEstimate
entries.summary: Covariance estimate using a long-run covariance estimator.
keywords:
Covariance estimate using a long-run covariance estimator.

Parameters
----------
short_run : ndarray
    The short-run covariance estimate.
one_sided_strict : ndarray
    The one-sided strict covariance estimate.
columns : Index or list of str, optional
    Column labels to use if covariance estimates are returned as
    DataFrames.
long_run : ndarray, optional
    The long-run covariance estimate. If not provided, computed from
    short_run and one_sided_strict.
one_sided : ndarray, optional
    The one-sided covariance estimate. If not provided, computed
    from short_run and one_sided_strict.

Notes
-----
If :math:`\Gamma_0` is the short-run covariance and :math:`\Lambda_1` is
the one-sided strict covariance, then the long-run covariance is defined

.. math::

    \Omega = \Gamma_0 + \Lambda_1 + \Lambda_1^H

and the one-sided covariance is

.. math::

    \Lambda_0 = \Gamma_0 + \Lambda_1.

:math:`^H` is the conjugate transpose, which is the transpose for real
estimates. The estimates of complex data are complex Hermitian matrices.

    if bandwidth_method is "andrews" and the bandwidth must be estimated but
    the AR(1) cannot be fitted to the columns of x with positive weight, for
    example because they are all constant.

Notes
-----
The kernel weights are defined by the concrete estimators that inherit from
this class. A kernel that is 0 beyond 1 uses :math:`z=\frac{h}{H+1}` for the
lags h that are smaller than :math:`H+1`, where H is the bandwidth, so that
H is the number of lags with a positive weight. The quadratic-spectral
kernel uses :math:`z=\frac{h}{H}` for every lag.

If the bandwidth is not provided, it is estimated using the constants of
[1]_ and either the automatic lag selection of [2]_, the default, or the
AR(1) plug-in estimate of [1]_ when ``bandwidth_method`` is "andrews". See
``opt_bandwidth`` for details.

**Complex data.** The estimators accept complex data, for which they are
Hermitian. The lag-:math:`j` autocovariance is
:math:`\hat{\Gamma}_j=T^{-1}\sum_t x_t x_{t-j}^H`, where :math:`^H` is the
conjugate transpose, :math:`\hat{\Gamma}_{-j}=\hat{\Gamma}_j^H`, and the
long-run covariance
:math:`\hat{\Omega}=\hat{\Gamma}_0+\sum_{j\geq 1}w_j(\hat{\Gamma}_j+
\hat{\Gamma}_j^H)` is a complex Hermitian matrix. If :math:`x_t=a_t+ib_t`,
then :math:`\hat{\Omega}=\hat{\Omega}_{aa}+\hat{\Omega}_{bb}+
i(\hat{\Omega}_{ba}-\hat{\Omega}_{ab})`, where :math:`\hat{\Omega}_{uv}` is
the long-run covariance of the real data :math:`u` and :math:`v` with the same
kernel and bandwidth. The automatic bandwidth combines the columns of x
using ``weights`` and uses the real part of the autocovariances of this
complex series. The pseudo-covariance :math:`E[x_t x_{t-j}^\prime]` is not
estimated, and the estimates are complex128 arrays. Real data give float64
estimates.

References
----------
.. [1] Andrews, D. W. K. (1991). Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation
   consistent covariance matrix estimation. Econometrica, 59(3), 817-858.
.. [2] Newey, W. K., & West, K. D. (1994). Automatic lag selection in
   covariance matrix estimation. Review of Economic Studies, 61(4), 631-653.

entries.name: arch.covariance.kernel.Gallant
entries.summary: Alternative name for Parzen covariance estimator.
keywords:
Alternative name for Parzen covariance estimator.

Parameters
----------
x : array_like
    The data to use in covariance estimation. Observations are in rows and
    variables in columns. Integer, Boolean and float32 data are converted to
    float64, and complex data to complex128. float16 data are not accepted.
    Must have at least 2 rows and 1 column, and must not contain NaN or
    infinite values.
bandwidth : float, optional
    The kernel's bandwidth.  If None, optimal bandwidth is estimated. Must
    be finite and non-negative.
df_adjust : int, optional
    Degrees of freedom to remove when adjusting the covariance. Uses the
    number of observations in x minus df_adjust when dividing
    inner-products. Must be at least 0 and smaller than the number of
    observations in x.
center : bool, optional
    A flag indicating whether x should be demeaned before estimating the
    covariance.
weights : array_like, optional
    An array of weights used to combine when estimating optimal bandwidth.
    If not provided, a vector of 1s is used. Must have nvar elements, be
    finite and non-negative, and at least one must be strictly positive.
force_int : bool, optional
    Force bandwidth to be an integer.
bandwidth_method : {"newey-west", "andrews"}, optional
    The method used to estimate the bandwidth when bandwidth is None.
    "newey-west" uses the nonparametric estimate of Newey and West (1994)
    and "andrews" uses the AR(1) plug-in estimate of Andrews (1991), see
    ``opt_bandwidth``. Not case sensitive, and hyphens and underscores are
    ignored as in the names of kernels, so that "newey_west" and
    "neweywest" are "newey-west". Ignored if bandwidth is provided, and by
    ZeroLag.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If x cannot be converted to float64 or complex128 (it is float16, or
    contains strings or objects that are not numbers), if weights cannot be
    converted to float64, if bandwidth is not a real number, if df_adjust is
    not an integer (a float, including 5.0, or a Boolean is not accepted), or
    if center or force_int is not a bool, or if bandwidth_method is not a str.
ValueError
    If x is not 2-d, has fewer than 2 rows or no columns or contains NaN or
    infinite values; if bandwidth is negative or not finite; if df_adjust
    is negative or not smaller than the number of observations; or if
    weights does not have nvar finite elements, has a negative element or
    has only zeros; if bandwidth_method is not one of the available names; or
    if bandwidth_method is "andrews" and the bandwidth must be estimated but
    the AR(1) cannot be fitted to the columns of x with positive weight, for
    example because they are all constant.

See Also
--------
Parzen : Kernel covariance estimator using the Parzen kernel.

entries.name: arch.covariance.var.PreWhitenedRecolored
entries.summary: VAR-HAC and Pre-Whitened-Recolored Long-run covariance estimation.
keywords:
VAR-HAC and Pre-Whitened-Recolored Long-run covariance estimation.

Andrews & Monahan [1]_ PWRC and DenHaan-Levin's VAR-HAC [2]_ covariance
estimators.

Parameters
----------
x : array_like
    The data to use in covariance estimation. Observations are in rows and
    variables in columns. Integer, Boolean and float32 data are converted to
    float64. float16 and complex data are not accepted. Must have at least 2
    rows and 1 column, and must not contain NaN or infinite values.
lags : int, optional
    The number of lags to include in the VAR. If None, a specification
    search is used to select the order. Must be non-negative and small
    enough that each equation of the VAR has more observations than
    parameters, see Notes.
method : {"aic", "hqc", "bic"}, optional
    The information criteria to use in the model specification search.
    Not case sensitive.
diagonal : bool, optional
    Flag indicating whether the specification search also considers
    models where the coefficient matrices on the final lags are
    diagonal. A diagonal coefficient matrix restricts all off-diagonal
    coefficients to be zero. Only used when lags is None and x has more
    than one column.
max_lag : int, optional
    The maximum lag to use in the model specification search. If None,
    then int(nobs**(1/3)) is used. Must be non-negative. The value used is
    limited, see Notes.
sample_autocov : bool, optional
    Whether to use the sample autocovariance of x or the autocovariance
    implied by the estimated VAR when computing the short-run and
    one-sided covariances. Does not affect the long-run covariance.
kernel : str or None, optional
    The name of the kernel to use, such as "bartlett" or
    "quadratic-spectral". It can be the name of any of the kernels in
    ``arch.covariance.kernel.KERNELS``, in lower case with hyphens between
    the words. The name is not case sensitive and any underscores or
    hyphens are ignored, so that "quadratic-spectral", "quadratic_spectral"
    and "quadraticspectral" are all the same. Use None to compute the VAR-HAC estimator, which
    recolors the residual covariance without applying a kernel to the
    residuals.
bandwidth : float, optional
    The kernel's bandwidth.  If None, optimal bandwidth is estimated
    from the VAR residuals. Must be finite and non-negative, and None or 0
    when kernel is None.
df_adjust : int, optional
    Degrees of freedom to remove when adjusting the covariance. Uses the
    number of observations in x minus df_adjust when dividing
    inner-products, see Notes. Must be at least 0 and smaller than the
    number of observations in x.
center : bool, optional
    A flag indicating whether x should be demeaned before estimating the
    covariance.
weights : array_like, optional
    An array of weights used to combine when estimating optimal bandwidth.
    If not provided, a vector of 1s is used. Must have nvar elements, be
    finite and non-negative, and at least one must be strictly positive.
force_int : bool, optional
    Force bandwidth to be an integer.
bandwidth_method : {"newey-west", "andrews"}, optional
    The method used to estimate the bandwidth of the VAR residuals when
    bandwidth is None. "newey-west" uses the nonparametric estimate of
    Newey & West (1994) and "andrews" uses the AR(1) plug-in estimate of
    Andrews (1991), see ``opt_bandwidth`` of the kernel estimators. Not case
    sensitive, and hyphens and underscores are ignored as in the names of
    kernels. Ignored if bandwidth is provided or kernel is None.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If x or weights cannot be converted to float64 (x is float16 or complex, or
    contains strings or objects that are not numbers), if lags, max_lag or
    df_adjust is not an integer (a float, including 5.0, or a Boolean is
    not accepted), if bandwidth is not a real number, if diagonal,
    sample_autocov, center or force_int is not a bool, or if method, kernel
    or bandwidth_method is not a str.
ValueError
    If x is not 2-d, has fewer than 2 rows or no columns or contains NaN or
    infinite values; if lags or max_lag is negative or lags is larger than
    the largest order that can be estimated; if bandwidth is negative, not
    finite or not None or 0 when kernel is None; if df_adjust is negative
    or not smaller than the number of observations; if weights does not
    have nvar finite non-negative elements, or has only zeros; if method,
    kernel or bandwidth_method is not one of the available names; or if
    bandwidth_method is "andrews" and the AR(1) cannot be fitted to the
    columns of the VAR residuals with positive weight, for example because
    they are all constant.

See Also
--------
arch.covariance.kernel
    Kernel-based long-run covariance estimators.

Notes
-----
The estimator is computed in three steps.

**Prewhitening.** A VAR is estimated by least squares, equation by
equation,

.. math::

   x_t = c + A_1 x_{t-1} + \ldots + A_P x_{t-P} + \epsilon_t

where the constant :math:`c` is included only when ``center`` is True.
When ``lags`` is provided, a VAR(``lags``) with unrestricted coefficient
matrices is used. Otherwise the order is selected by minimizing

.. math::

   IC = \ln|\hat{\Sigma}| + \lambda \frac{k}{T}

where :math:`\hat{\Sigma}=T^{-1}\sum_t \hat{\epsilon}_t\hat{\epsilon}_t^\prime`,
:math:`k` is the total number of estimated parameters, :math:`T` is the
number of observations used in the regressions, which is common to all
candidate models, and :math:`\lambda` is 2 (``"aic"``),
:math:`2\ln\ln T` (``"hqc"``) or :math:`\ln T` (``"bic"``). Models with
0, 1, ..., ``max_lag`` lags are considered. When ``diagonal`` is True
and x has more than one column, the search also considers models with
unrestricted coefficient matrices on the first :math:`p` lags and
diagonal coefficient matrices on lags :math:`p+1, \ldots, q` for
:math:`p < q \leq` ``max_lag``, so that each series only uses its own
values at the additional lags. ``max_lag`` is limited to
``(nobs - nvar) // nvar`` and to the largest order for which each equation
of the VAR has more observations than parameters. ``lags`` must also
satisfy this restriction.

**Kernel estimation.** The long-run covariance of the VAR residuals,
:math:`\hat{\Omega}_\epsilon`, is estimated using the selected kernel
applied to the residuals without centering. The automatic bandwidth is
estimated from the residuals using ``bandwidth_method``. When ``kernel`` is None, a
zero-lag kernel is used so that
:math:`\hat{\Omega}_\epsilon=\hat{\Sigma}`, which is the VAR-HAC
estimator of den Haan & Levin. This is also the case when the bandwidth is
0. The products of the residuals are divided by :math:`T-` ``df_adjust``,
where :math:`T` is the number of observations in x, rather than by the
number of residuals, which is smaller when the order is positive. This
matches the ``sandwich`` package in R: the estimator is identical to
``sandwich::meatHAC(prewhite=P, adjust=FALSE)`` when ``df_adjust`` is 0
and to ``sandwich::meatHAC(prewhite=P, adjust=TRUE)`` when ``df_adjust`` is
the number of columns in x, if the kernel weights are the same, x has been
demeaned and ``center`` is False, since the VAR in R has no intercept.

**Recoloring.** The long-run covariance of x is

.. math::

   \hat{\Omega} = \hat{D}\hat{\Omega}_\epsilon\hat{D}^\prime,
   \quad \hat{D} = \left(I_N - \sum_{i=1}^P \hat{A}_i\right)^{-1}

where :math:`N` is the number of columns in x. When the selected order
is 0, no VAR is estimated and all returned values are those of the
kernel estimator applied to x (demeaned when ``center`` is True).

When the VAR order is positive, the returned
:class:`~arch.covariance.kernel.CovarianceEstimate` contains

* ``long_run``: :math:`\hat{\Omega}`.
* ``short_run``: the upper-left :math:`N` by :math:`N` block of
  :math:`\Gamma_0`, the covariance of the stacked vector
  :math:`[x_t^\prime, \ldots, x_{t-P+1}^\prime]^\prime`. By default
  :math:`\Gamma_0` is implied by the estimated VAR and the covariance of
  its residuals, :math:`\hat{\Sigma}`, so that ``short_run`` is the
  variance of x implied by the VAR. When ``sample_autocov`` is True,
  :math:`\Gamma_0` is computed from the sample autocovariances of x and
  ``short_run`` is the sample variance of x. It is not the covariance of
  the VAR residuals, which is available as :attr:`resid_cov`.
* ``one_sided_strict``: the upper-left :math:`N` by :math:`N` block of
  :math:`F(I-F)^{-1}\Gamma_0` where :math:`F` is the companion-form
  coefficient matrix of the VAR. This is
  :math:`\sum_{j\geq 1}\Gamma_j` where :math:`\Gamma_j=E[x_tx_{t-j}^\prime]`.
* ``one_sided``: ``short_run`` plus ``one_sided_strict``.

The one-sided covariances do not use the kernel. The identities in
:class:`~arch.covariance.kernel.CovarianceEstimate` that define the
one-sided covariances hold, so that
``one_sided = short_run + one_sided_strict``. The long-run covariance
satisfies ``long_run = short_run + one_sided_strict + one_sided_strict.T``
when the autocovariances are those of the VAR and the kernel is not used,
that is when ``sample_autocov`` is False and ``kernel`` is None or the
bandwidth is 0. Otherwise ``long_run`` differs from this sum.

**Complex data are not supported.** The kernel estimators in
:mod:`arch.covariance.kernel` accept complex data, but this estimator raises a
``TypeError``. Prewhitening fits a model, and there is no single VAR for complex
data. A VAR with complex coefficients cannot represent real and imaginary parts
that depend on each other in a way that is not a complex multiplication, and the
VAR of the stacked real and imaginary parts is a different model with more
parameters. The order that the information criteria above select depends on
which of them is used. To prewhiten complex data, use this estimator with
``np.column_stack([x.real, x.imag])``, or use a kernel estimator, which needs no
model.

**Inspecting the VAR.** The prewhitening step determines the estimate, so
its results are available. :attr:`order` is the order of the VAR, which is
the only way to learn which order was chosen when ``lags`` is None.
:attr:`resid` are the residuals of the VAR, which are the series that the
kernel is applied to and can be tested to check that the VAR removed the
serial correlation in x. :attr:`resid_cov` is their covariance, which is
the matrix that is recolored into the long-run covariance of x. None of
these require the VAR to be covariance stationary, so they are available
even when :attr:`cov` raises an error because it is not.

References
----------
.. [1] Andrews, D. W., & Monahan, J. C. (1992). An improved
   heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix
   estimator. Econometrica: Journal of the Econometric Society, 953-966.
.. [2] Haan, W. J. D., & Levin, A. T. (2000). Robust covariance matrix
   estimation with data-dependent VAR prewhitening order (No. 255).
   National Bureau of Economic Research.

entries.name: arch.unitroot.ADF
entries.summary: Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit root test.
keywords:
Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit root test.

Parameters
----------
y : array_like
    The data to test for a unit root.
lags : int, optional
    The number of lags to use in the ADF regression.  If omitted or None,
    `method` is used to automatically select the lag length with no more
    than `max_lags` lags included.
trend : {"n", "c", "ct", "ctt"}, optional
    The trend component to include in the test. Not case sensitive.

    - "n" - No trend components
    - "c" - Include a constant
    - "ct" - Include a constant and linear time trend
    - "ctt" - Include a constant and linear and quadratic time trends

max_lags : int, optional
    The maximum number of lags to use when selecting lag length. If
    omitted or None, the maximum number of lags is 12 * (nobs/100) ** (1/4),
    rounded up, reduced when needed in short samples.
method : {"aic", "bic", "t-stat", "maic"}, optional
    The method to use when selecting the lag length. Not case sensitive.

    - "aic" - Select the minimum of the Akaike IC
    - "bic" - Select the minimum of the Schwarz/Bayesian IC
    - "t-stat" - Select the largest lag length for which the t-statistic
      of the last lag is significant, using a cut-off of 1.645 for the
      absolute value of the t-statistic
    - "maic" - Select the minimum of Ng and Perron's modified Akaike IC ([5]_)

low_memory : bool, optional
    Flag indicating whether to use a low memory implementation of the
    lag selection algorithm. The low memory algorithm is slower than
    the standard algorithm but will use 2-4% of the memory required for
    the standard algorithm. This options allows automatic lag selection
    to be used in very long time series. If None, the low memory algorithm
    is used when the series has more than 100,000 observations.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `y` cannot be converted to numbers, `lags` or `max_lags` is not an
    integer, `low_memory` is not a bool or None, or `trend` or `method` is not
    a str.
ValueError
    If `y` is not 1-d or contains NaN or inf, `lags` or `max_lags` is
    negative, or `trend` or `method` is not one of the options.
InfeasibleTestException
    If `y` is constant or has too few observations for `trend`, or `lags` or
    `max_lags` is larger than the observations can support. A regression with
    `lags` lags needs at least 3 + 2 * `lags` + the number of trend terms
    observations. This is also a ``ValueError``.

Notes
-----
The null hypothesis of the Augmented Dickey-Fuller is that there is a unit
root, with the alternative that there is no unit root. If the pvalue is
above a critical size, then the null cannot be rejected and the series
appears to be a unit root.

The p-values are from an approximation of the asymptotic distribution of the
statistic that follows the methodology of MacKinnon (1994), and are a smooth
and increasing function of the statistic. The critical values are from
response surface regressions that follow the methodology of MacKinnon (2010),
and depend on the number of observations. Both are fit to the same new
simulations, and the p-values of the asymptotic critical values are 1%, 5% and
10%.
If the p-value is close to significant, then the critical values should be
used to judge whether to reject the null.

The autolag option and maxlag for it are described in Greene [1]_.
See Hamilton [2]_ for more on ADF tests. Critical value simulation based
on MacKinnon [3]_ and [4]_.

References
----------
.. [1] Greene, W. H. 2011. Econometric Analysis. Prentice Hall: Upper
   Saddle River, New Jersey.

.. [2] Hamilton, J. D. 1994. Time Series Analysis. Princeton: Princeton
   University Press.

.. [3] MacKinnon, J.G. 1994.  "Approximate asymptotic distribution
   functions for unit-root and cointegration tests.  `Journal of
   Business and Economic Statistics` 12, 167-76.

.. [4] MacKinnon, J.G. 2010. "Critical Values for Cointegration Tests."
   Queen's University, Dept of Economics, Working Papers.  Available at
   https://ideas.repec.org/p/qed/wpaper/1227.html
.. [5] Ng, S., and P. Perron. 2001. "Lag Length Selection and the
   Construction of Unit Root Tests with Good Size and Power."
   Econometrica 69, 1519-1554.

entries.name: arch.unitroot.DFGLS
entries.summary: Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock's ([ers]_) GLS detrended Dickey-Fuller.
keywords:
Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock's ([ers]_) GLS detrended Dickey-Fuller.

Parameters
----------
y : array_like
    The data to test for a unit root.
lags : int, optional
    The number of lags to use in the ADF regression.  If omitted or None,
    `method` is used to automatically select the lag length with no more
    than `max_lags` lags included.
trend : {"c", "ct"}, optional
    The trend component to include in the test. Not case sensitive.

    - "c" - Include a constant
    - "ct" - Include a constant and linear time trend

max_lags : int, optional
    The maximum number of lags to use when selecting lag length. When using
    automatic lag length selection, the lag is selected using OLS
    detrending rather than GLS detrending ([pq]_). If omitted or None,
    the maximum number of lags is 12 * (nobs/100) ** (1/4), rounded up,
    reduced when needed in short samples.
method : {"aic", "bic", "t-stat", "maic"}, optional
    The method to use when selecting the lag length. Not case sensitive.

    - "aic" - Select the minimum of the Akaike IC
    - "bic" - Select the minimum of the Schwarz/Bayesian IC
    - "t-stat" - Select the largest lag length for which the t-statistic
      of the last lag is significant, using a cut-off of 1.645 for the
      absolute value of the t-statistic
    - "maic" - Select the minimum of Ng and Perron's modified Akaike IC ([np]_)

low_memory : bool, optional
    Flag indicating whether to use a low memory implementation of the
    lag selection algorithm. The low memory algorithm is slower than
    the standard algorithm but will use 2-4% of the memory required for
    the standard algorithm. This options allows automatic lag selection
    to be used in very long time series. If None, the low memory algorithm
    is used when the series has at least 100,000 observations.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `y` cannot be converted to numbers, `lags` or `max_lags` is not an
    integer, `low_memory` is not a bool or None, or `trend` or `method` is not
    a str.
ValueError
    If `y` is not 1-d or contains NaN or inf, `lags` or `max_lags` is
    negative, or `trend` or `method` is not one of the options.
InfeasibleTestException
    If `y` is constant or has too few observations for `trend`, or `lags` or
    `max_lags` is larger than the observations can support. A regression with
    `lags` lags needs at least 3 + 2 * `lags` observations. This is also a
    ``ValueError``.

Notes
-----
The null hypothesis of the Dickey-Fuller GLS is that there is a unit
root, with the alternative that there is no unit root. If the pvalue is
above a critical size, then the null cannot be rejected and the series
appears to be a unit root.

DFGLS differs from the ADF test in that an initial GLS detrending step
is used before a trend-less ADF regression is run.

Critical values and p-values when trend is "c" are identical to
the ADF.  When trend is set to "ct", they are from novel simulations.

References
----------
.. [ers] Elliott, G. R., T. J. Rothenberg, and J. H. Stock. 1996. Efficient
       tests for an autoregressive unit root. Econometrica 64: 813-836
.. [pq] Perron, P., & Qu, Z. (2007). A simple modification to improve the
       finite sample properties of Ng and Perron's unit root tests.
       Economics letters, 94(1), 12-19.
.. [np] Ng, S., and P. Perron. 2001. "Lag Length Selection and the
       Construction of Unit Root Tests with Good Size and Power."
       Econometrica 69, 1519-1554.

entries.name: arch.unitroot.KPSS
entries.summary: Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt and Shin (KPSS) stationarity test.
keywords:
Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt and Shin (KPSS) stationarity test.

Parameters
----------
y : array_like
    The data to test for stationarity.
lags : int, optional
    The number of lags to use in the Newey-West estimator of the long-run
    covariance.  If omitted or None, the number of lags is calculated
    with the data-dependent method of Hobijn et al. (1998). See also
    Andrews (1991), Newey & West (1994), and Schwert (1989).
    Set lags=-1 to use the old method that only depends on the sample
    size, 12 * (nobs/100) ** (1/4).
trend : {"c", "ct"}, optional
    The trend component to include in the test. Not case sensitive.

    - "c" - Include a constant
    - "ct" - Include a constant and linear time trend

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `y` cannot be converted to numbers, `lags` is not an integer or None,
    or `trend` is not a str.
ValueError
    If `y` is not 1-d or contains NaN or inf, `lags` is less than -1, or
    `trend` is not one of the options.
InfeasibleTestException
    If `y` is constant or has too few observations for `trend`, or `lags`
    (the number from the rule 12 * (nobs/100) ** (1/4) if it is -1) is
    larger than the number of observations in y. This is also a
    ``ValueError``.

Notes
-----
The null hypothesis of the KPSS test is that the series is weakly
stationary and the alternative is that it is non-stationary.
If the p-value is above a critical size, then the null cannot be
rejected and the series appears stationary.

The p-values and critical values were computed using an extensive
simulation based on 100,000,000 replications using series with 2,000
observations. See [3]_ for the initial description of the KPSS test.
Further details are available in [2]_ and [5]_. Details about the long-run
covariance estimation can be found in [1]_ and [4]_.

References
----------
.. [1] Andrews, D.W.K. (1991). "Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation
       consistent covariance matrix estimation". Econometrica, 59: 817-858.

.. [2] Hobijn, B., Frances, B.H., & Ooms, M. (2004). Generalizations
       of the KPSS-test for stationarity. Statistica Neerlandica, 52: 483-502.

.. [3] Kwiatkowski, D.; Phillips, P. C. B.; Schmidt, P.; Shin, Y. (1992).
       "Testing the null hypothesis of stationarity against the alternative of
       a unit root". Journal of Econometrics 54 (1-3), 159-178

.. [4] Newey, W.K., & West, K.D. (1994). "Automatic lag selection in
       covariance matrix estimation". Review of Economic Studies, 61: 631-653.

.. [5] Schwert, G. W. (1989). "Tests for unit roots: A Monte Carlo
       investigation". Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 7 (2):
       147-159.

entries.name: arch.unitroot.PhillipsPerron
entries.summary: Phillips-Perron unit root test.
keywords:
Phillips-Perron unit root test.

Parameters
----------
y : array_like
    The data to test for a unit root.
lags : int, optional
    The number of lags to use in the Newey-West estimator of the long-run
    covariance.  If omitted or None, the lag length is set automatically to
    12 * (nobs/100) ** (1/4), rounded up.
trend : {"n", "c", "ct"}, optional
    The trend component to include in the test. Not case sensitive.

    - "n" - No trend components
    - "c" - Include a constant
    - "ct" - Include a constant and linear time trend

test_type : {"tau", "rho"}, optional
    The test to use when computing the test statistic. Not case sensitive.
    "tau" is based on the t-stat and "rho" uses a test based on nobs times
    the re-centered regression coefficient.

Raises
------
TypeError
    If `y` cannot be converted to numbers, `lags` is not an integer, or
    `trend` or `test_type` is not a str.
ValueError
    If `y` is not 1-d or contains NaN or inf, `lags` is negative, or `trend`
    or `test_type` is not one of the options.
InfeasibleTestException
    If `y` is constant or has too few observations for `trend`, or `lags`
    (the default number of lags if it is None) is larger than the number of
    observations in y minus 1. This is also a ``ValueError``.

Notes
-----
The null hypothesis of the Phillips-Perron (PP) test is that there is a
unit root, with the alternative that there is no unit root. If the pvalue
is above a critical size, then the null cannot be rejected and the series
appears to be a unit root.

Unlike the ADF test, the regression estimated includes only one lag of
the dependent variable, in addition to trend terms. Any serial
correlation in the regression errors is accounted for using a long-run
variance estimator (currently Newey-West).

See Philips and Perron for details [3]_. See Hamilton [1]_ for more on
PP tests. Newey and West contains information about long-run variance
estimation [2]_. The p-values are obtained through regression surface
approximation using the methodology of MacKinnon [4]_ and [5]_, only
using many more simulations.

If the p-value is close to significant, then the critical values should be
used to judge whether to reject the null.

References
----------
.. [1] Hamilton, J. D. 1994. Time Series Analysis. Princeton: Princeton
       University Press.

.. [2] Newey, W. K., and K. D. West. 1987. "A simple, positive
       semidefinite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance
       matrix". Econometrica 55, 703-708.

.. [3] Phillips, P. C. B., and P. Perron. 1988. "Testing for a unit root in
       time series regression". Biometrika 75, 335-346.

.. [4] MacKinnon, J.G. 1994.  "Approximate asymptotic distribution
       functions for unit-root and cointegration tests".  Journal of
       Business and  Economic Statistics. 12, 167-76.

.. [5] MacKinnon, J.G. 2010. "Critical Values for Cointegration Tests."
       Queen's University, Dept of Economics, Working Papers.  Available at
       https://ideas.repec.org/p/qed/wpaper/1227.html
